name: Benin Bronzes
what: Thousands of brass and bronze plaques, heads and figures cast by the royal guild of the Kingdom of Benin, in today's Nigeria, from about the 13th century; many of the plaques were cast in the 16th and 17th centuries.
why: A collection, not one object, but it moved as one: European brass came in as trade, was melted into royal art, left in one week of looting in 1897, and scattered to museums worldwide. It is the clearest case of returns now under way.
now: Scattered across 160 or more museums. Germany transferred ownership of about 1,100 to Nigeria in 2022; the Horniman Museum, the Smithsonian and others have returned theirs. The British Museum holds over 900.
dispute: Nigeria and the Oba of Benin ask for their return. The British Museum says the British Museum Act prevents it from giving them away.

sources.cite: Hicks, D. (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. Pluto Press.
Plankensteiner, B. (ed.) (2007). Benin: Kings and Rituals. Snoeck.

stops.note: Lead-isotope tests (Skowronek et al. 2023) show that much of the brass in 16th-century Benin plaques came from Rhineland manillas, the horseshoe-shaped brass bracelets the Portuguese used as money on the West African coast.
stops.meet: a brass worker in the Rhineland

stops.note: Manillas were shipped out through Lisbon by the hundred thousand to buy pepper, ivory and enslaved people on the Guinea coast.
The guild of brass casters on Igun Street melted the metal and cast it by the lost-wax method into plaques for the pillars of the Oba's palace, showing kings, warriors and Portuguese traders.
stops.meet: a caster of the Igun Eronmwon guild, or a courtier at the Oba's palace

stops.note: In February 1897 a British punitive expedition of about 1,200 men burned Benin City and took around 3,000-10,000 objects from the palace and shrines, in reprisal for the killing of a British party in January.
stops.meet: a member of the Benin court in February 1897

stops.owner: Foreign Office, British Museum, private buyers
stops.note: Some 300 plaques went to the British Museum; much of the rest was sold at auction, partly to pay for the expedition, and given out as officers' souvenirs.
German museums bought heavily on the London market; by 1900 Berlin held one of the largest collections of all.

In December 2022 Germany's foreign minister handed back 20 bronzes in Abuja, after transferring ownership of all Benin objects in German public museums (about 1,100) to Nigeria. In 2023 Nigeria's president vested ownership in the Oba of Benin.
